notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Long yellow plates with the blue EU strip on the left, front and back. Taxis have blue plates.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Extremely flat, often reclaimed land at or below sea level, with canals, ditches, dikes, dams and bridges everywhere.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Almost no street-level utility poles at all; Belgium uses them fairly often.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Simple white bollard with a red reflector. Rarely round French-style ones with a red band that does not fully wrap.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Reddish-pink bike lanes beside roads, and cyclists everywhere.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: White lines like most of Europe, with dashed outside lines, and sometimes a unique green middle line.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Brick-paved roads are common, plus brick-style rumble strips along rural road edges that are fairly unique.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Speed bumps have white warning stripes alternating long and short.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Sidewalks use square grey tiles in an offset pattern; historic areas may use small bricks.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Street signs are almost always blue with white letters, and names often end in -straat, -weg, -laan, -pad or -plein.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Direction and town entry signs are blue with white lettering; entry signs can be elaborate and often name the municipality after "gemeente".

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Green road markers with the road number in a small box: red and starting with A for motorways, yellow and starting with N for regional roads.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Sign edges wrap around to the back, giving a border visible from behind. This is consistent and unique.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Signposts often have black-and-white or blue-and-white stripes; bulky yellow posts on traffic islands.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Many double vowels and clusters like ij, ieuw and oe; "IJ" as one capital letter is unique. Also spoken in northern Belgium.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Red-brown brick buildings with orange or dark grey tiled roofs; nearly half of homes are row houses. Master-planned, tidy suburbs.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Rural roads lined with rows of trees, and windmills, old and modern, are common.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Marshy polder landscape with many small waterways; the south and east look more like typical flat farmland.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Low hills in the far south of this province, rare in a flat country.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Unusually forested central area with heath, sandy soil and slight elevation.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Land reclaimed from the sea: very straight roads, huge crop fields, wind turbines and no historic buildings.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: A regional language with circumflex vowels (Â Ê Ô Û) and more Y; bilingual town signs and street names ending -wei or -strjitte.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The North Sea coast is lined with dunes, and the northwestern islands are busy tourist spots with sandy dunes.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Farms in the north often have very large roofs.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Rolling shutters on house windows are more common in the southern half. Use with caution.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: White stickers on street lights: long and vertical with 3 to 4 digits in the far southeast; horizontal with 1 or 2 digits in the southern province next to it.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Greenhouses cover most of the land in a municipality southwest of The Hague.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: A very long straight dam with a divided highway, water on the southeast side and a dike on the northwest.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: A huge harbour with heavy industry and round fuel tanks stretches from the big southern city to the sea.
